extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, petitioners, and patent litigators practicing before the U.S. Patent Office (IPR filings)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and procedural standards for preparing and filing an Inter Partes Review (IPR) petition challenging U.S. patent claims, including eligibility, formatting, required contents, evidence, and strategic drafting considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility to file an IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: A person who is not the owner of the patent (the petitioner) may initiate an IPR, but an IPR is not available to: the owner of the patent; a petitioner or real party-in-interest who filed a civil action in federal district court challenging validity of a claim (with a limited exception for counterclaims); a petitioner/real-party-in-interest/party-in-privity who has not filed the IPR within one year of being served with an infringement complaint; or a petitioner/real-party-in-interest/party-in-privity who is estopped from challenging the claim(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 35 U.S.C. §§312, 315, and 37 C.F.R. §42.101. Careful pre-filing clearance is required to ensure no prior civil action, timing, or estoppel bars the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for filing an IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: An IPR may be filed after termination of a post-grant review or after a patent has been issued for more than nine months, whichever is later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confirm the patent's issuance/post-grant review dates to ensure the petition is timely under statutory timing rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Petition format and page/font/margin limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Petition must be less than 60 pages in 8½ by 11 inch pages; text must be double spaced and in at least a 14-point proportional font with no more than 4 characters per centimeter and margins of no less than 1 inch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page limit does not include a table of contents, table of authorities, certificate of service, or appendix of exhibits. See 37 C.F.R. §§42.6 and 42.24. Strictly adhere to these formatting rules to avoid procedural rejection or sanctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees required to obtain filing
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain a filing date, the petition must include the petition fee: $9,000 request fee, $14,000 institution fee, and $200 per claim over 20.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See 35 U.S.C. §312 and 37 C.F.R.§§ 42.103, 42.15. Ensure correct payment and fee categorization to secure the filing date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification of IPR availability and non-bar/estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: The petition must include a certification that the patent at issue is available for an IPR and that the petitioner is not barred or estopped from requesting an IPR for the patent at issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a formal requirement tied to eligibility; mistaken or unsupported certifications risk dismissal or estoppel consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of precise relief requested and per-claim requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: For each claim challenged, the petition must state the precise relief requested and include: a construction of the claim (including references to the patent specification for some claim formats); the statutory grounds for the challenge (35 U.S.C. §102 and/or §103); and a discussion of the invalidity of the claim specifying where each claim element is found in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear claim constructions and tie each element to prior art; ambiguous or generalized arguments weaken the petition and risk exclusion of evidence. See 35 U.S.C. ¶312 and 37 C.F.R. §42.104.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence citation and specificity requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The petition must include references to evidence by exhibit number, state the relevance of the evidence to the respective validity challenge, and reference the specific portions of the evidence that support the challenge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PTAB may exclude or give no weight to evidence where the petitioner fails to state its relevance or identify specific portions that support the challenge (35 U.S.C. ¶312(a)(3) and 37 C.F.R. §42.104(b)(5)). Be explicit about which document pages/lines support each claim element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of claim charts (recommended evidence organization)
rubrics_metrics.description: A two-column claim chart with claim elements in the left column and the corresponding quotation or specific reference in the right column is a useful guide for the Board in evaluating claims against prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt claim charts to clearly map claim elements to specific prior-art passages or exhibits; this improves clarity and helps prevent exclusion for lack of specificity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on documentary evidence and prior testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to prior art, rely on other documentary evidence (e.g., prior litigation testimony if available) as exhibits to the petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assemble and number exhibits carefully; documentary evidence can be pivotal given limited IPR discovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity and role of expert declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert declarations are useful and in most cases important for explaining the prior art or other evidence; attorney argument will not take the place of expert testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include expert declarations as exhibits to the petition to explain technical aspects, interpret prior art, and provide opinions that attorneys cannot substitute for; declare qualifications and link the expert statements to exhibits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution standard (35 U.S.C. §314)
rubrics_metrics.description: The drafting goal is to convince the Director there 'is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner will prevail with respect to at least 1' of the patent claims challenged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target the petition to meet the §314 reasonable-likelihood threshold, but recognize that petitions should, when possible, be drafted to do more than just clear this bar to create a substantive trial record advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic drafting: do more than obtain institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the petitioner speaks first and IPR discovery is constrained, the Petition is the petitioner's opportunity to create a well-supported, strong impression of invalidity that will put the patentee at a disadvantage; petitioners should draft and include exhibits to go beyond just obtaining institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given timing and discovery constraints, use the petition to build a full evidentiary record and persuasive argumentation; think ahead to how the petition will shape the later trial and limit patentee's early rebuttal options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof and practical advantage for single-reference §102 challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden is on the petitioner to prove invalidity by a preponderance of the evidence, but where the challenge is based on a single piece of prior art under 35 U.S.C. §102, the patentee faces a difficult task in rebuttal because evidence-based rebuttal generally cannot be filed until after institution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the tactical advantage of strong single-reference §102 arguments and the importance of thoroughly documenting and evidencing such arguments in the petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Service of the Petition
rubrics_metrics.description: After preparation and filing, a Petition must be served on the appropriate party pursuant to 37 C.F.R. §§42.6 and 42.105.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure proper service procedures are followed post-filing to comply with regulatory requirements and avoid service-related defects.
